analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau, 35.5% of firms in educational services (NAICS 61) reported using AI in the last two weeks, up from 33.8% in the prior period. This is the share answering yes to the survey's AI use question.

The Department of Education's inventory of AI use cases shows a range of deployments. It lists CAISY for real-time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation, Grammarly for writing assistance, Otter.AI for transcription, and AWS Bedrock for building applications with foundation models. Other listed uses include generating summaries and outlines, code snippets in multiple languages, R code for data analysis, mock data sets, outreach strategies, and filters for prohibited prompts.

HolonIQ tracks the education economy, including EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher education, and workforce learning. The excerpt does not provide specific funding amounts or vendor concentration figures. The Department of Education inventory names Grammarly, Otter.AI, and AWS Bedrock as tools in use, but no spending data is reported.

No source in this set reports quantified return on investment. The Department of Education's inventory describes expected benefits such as reducing costs and boosting productivity for CAISY, but these are stated capabilities rather than measured outcomes. The course catalog on this site also does not report enrollment numbers or completion rates.

On risk and regulation, the Department of Education's guidance emphasizes responsible and secure usage, adherence to federal regulations, and alignment with the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. Its inventory includes data loss prevention and filters for prohibited prompt information, indicating attention to misuse controls.

The course catalog tracked on this site lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, with 3 offering public companion code. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry providers including DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and Andrej Karpathy. This catalog shows the training pathways the field currently uses, though it does not report which courses are most widely taken.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
